questions.prompt: What does a Hugging Face Hub repo id like `google-bert/bert-base-uncased` identify?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: The organization (or user) and the specific model repo within the Hub's git-backed registry

A repo id is `org/name` — it identifies exactly which organization or user published the repo and which model/dataset/Space it is, the same way a package name identifies a library.
keyPoints: A repo id is `org/name` — it identifies exactly which organization or user published the repo and which model/dataset/Space it is, the same way a package name identifies a library.

questions.prompt: Why is checking the license of a model just as important as checking its accuracy?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: A model can be technically excellent but legally restricted from the use you have in mind, such as commercial deployment

Two models can perform similarly well but carry very different licenses — one permissive, one restricted to research or requiring specific attribution. Skipping this check can create legal exposure later.
keyPoints: Two models can perform similarly well but carry very different licenses — one permissive, one restricted to research or requiring specific attribution.
Skipping this check can create legal exposure later.

questions.prompt: Why is processing a batch of 32 sentences together typically much faster than processing them one at a time?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Hardware like GPUs is built for parallel matrix operations, so a batch of many examples often takes roughly the same time as a single example, up to some size

GPUs excel at parallel tensor operations. Processing many sequences as one batched tensor exploits that parallelism, so throughput per example goes up dramatically compared to one-at-a-time processing.
keyPoints: GPUs excel at parallel tensor operations.
Processing many sequences as one batched tensor exploits that parallelism, so throughput per example goes up dramatically compared to one-at-a-time processing.

questions.prompt: What does `dataset.map(tokenize_fn, batched=True)` do?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Applies tokenize_fn across the dataset, passing batches of examples at a time, and returns a new dataset with the results

map() runs the given function across the dataset (in batches, when batched=True) and returns a new dataset containing the transformed results — commonly used to tokenize an entire dataset at once.
keyPoints: map() runs the given function across the dataset (in batches, when batched=True) and returns a new dataset containing the transformed results — commonly used to tokenize an entire dataset at once.

questions.prompt: What does the `Trainer` class package together?
questions.referenceAnswer: Trainer wraps the same training loop concepts from the deep learning course (forward/backward/optimizer step) together with checkpointing, logging, and evaluation, so you configure it rather than write the loop by hand.
keyPoints: Trainer wraps the same training loop concepts from the deep learning course (forward/backward/optimizer step) together with checkpointing, logging, and evaluation, so you configure it rather than write the loop by hand.

choices.text: Only the dataset loading logic
The training loop (forward pass, loss, backward pass, optimizer step) plus checkpointing, logging, and evaluation, all behind a configuration object
Only the model architecture
A brand new kind of optimizer not seen elsewhere

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of periodically saving checkpoints during training?
questions.referenceAnswer: Checkpoints are periodic snapshots of model and optimizer state. If training is interrupted, you can resume from the last checkpoint instead of losing all progress and starting over.
keyPoints: Checkpoints are periodic snapshots of model and optimizer state.
If training is interrupted, you can resume from the last checkpoint instead of losing all progress and starting over.

choices.text: Checkpoints have no practical purpose
They protect against losing all training progress if a crash, timeout, or bad run interrupts training
Checkpoints only exist to slow down training
Checkpoints replace the need for a validation set

questions.prompt: What does quantization do to a model's weights?
questions.referenceAnswer: Quantization represents each weight with fewer bits, directly shrinking memory footprint — the tradeoff is a small amount of numeric precision lost in exchange for a large memory savings.
keyPoints: Quantization represents each weight with fewer bits, directly shrinking memory footprint — the tradeoff is a small amount of numeric precision lost in exchange for a large memory savings.

choices.text: It deletes weights entirely to save space
It stores weights using fewer bits per number (e.g. 8-bit or 4-bit instead of 32-bit), trading some precision for a large reduction in memory footprint
It converts weights into text strings
It has no effect on memory usage

questions.prompt: What does `trainer.push_to_hub(repo_id)` upload?
questions.referenceAnswer: push_to_hub bundles up everything needed to reload the model elsewhere — weights, config, and tokenizer — and uploads it to the specified Hub repo.
keyPoints: push_to_hub bundles up everything needed to reload the model elsewhere — weights, config, and tokenizer — and uploads it to the specified Hub repo.

choices.text: Only the training logs, nothing else
The model weights, config, and tokenizer to a new or existing Hub repo
Nothing — push_to_hub only validates the model without uploading
Only the dataset used for training

questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Pin the exact model revision and compare a fixed test input. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Pin the exact model revision and compare a fixed test input.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.
